/en/architecture-with-ai/review-ai-gener.title: AI drafted an HLD — how do you check whether it is useful?
/en/architecture-with-ai/review-ai-gener.text: Tutorial 01 · about 12 minutes. Practice-inspired educational scenario. This is a model scenario, not an account of a particular client deployment or incident. Response excerpts below are editorial examples, not transcripts from a named model. AI drafted an HLD. Is it ready for implementation? The document looks convincing: components, a queue, a database and a diagram. That starts a useful conversation. The architect still needs to identify what came from the brief, what the model assumed and where the design could fail. A readable drawing does not establish that requirements are met. 1. Start with a brief you can inspect Copy this brief: We are designing a small appointment-booking service. Users select a slot on the web. The backend stores the booking in a database. A separate worker sends an informational email through an external provider. Email delivery is not a condition for accepting a booking. There are no payments. Scale, response-time targets and sign-in rules have not been decided. Do not invent these as facts. Use model data. Organisation names, personal data, internal addresses and confidential documents need handling rules set by your organisation. Define the session goal: a draft for review, rather than an approved architecture. 2. Ask for questions before a solution Separate facts, assumptions and unknowns. List five questions whose answers would most change the design. Explain the architectural impact of each. Do not choose vendors or products yet. Check whether AI asks about competing bookings for the same slot, user identification, data and retention, and availability requirements. Screen colours can wait. Mark missing decisions instead of answering on behalf of the business. 3. Draft the design and challenge it with a failure Draft a short HLD from the brief, marking assumptions explicitly. Compare synchronous and asynchronous email delivery. Explain what happens when the email provider fails. Include a simple Mermaid flowchart TB. Do not claim that a queue alone guarantees delivery. An example excerpt that needs review: “After storing the booking, the backend publishes a message to the queue. The queue ensures no notification is lost.” There is a gap: the process can terminate after committing the booking but before publishing. A queue alone does not solve a dual write. Ask AI to examine that exact gap rather than saying “improve the HLD”. The process terminates after the booking commits to the database but before the message reaches the queue. What persists? What can be lost? How would we detect it? Propose a mechanism, its costs and a verification test. 4. Fix the mechanism, not just the wording One option is a transactional outbox: the booking and notification task are stored in the same database transaction. A separate process reads tasks, publishes them and handles retries. This is not automatically the best choice for every system; justify it against the requirement for notification loss. Retries can deliver duplicates. Define an event identifier, duplicate-processing behaviour, retry limits and a path for manual resolution. The email provider may not support deduplication; do not promise exactly one email in that case. 5. Review the diagram separately flowchart TB User["User"] --> API["Booking API"] API --> DB["Database: booking and outbox"] DB --> Relay["Task publisher"] Relay --> Queue["Notification queue"] Queue --> Worker["Email worker"] Worker --> Provider["Email provider"] This is a simplified flow view. The database-to-publisher arrow represents task reads, not the database actively calling the publisher. Network boundaries and full security controls are omitted. Check two things independently: whether the syntax renders in your Mermaid version, and whether dependencies match the text. If parsing fails, download the Markdown and preserve the original block. Provide only the diagram and parser error for repair, without a confidential brief. Ask for the same components and relationships, then render again. Changing models does not replace this check. 6. Finish with evidence and a decision Terminate the process between committing a booking and publishing. The task should remain recoverable. Disable the email provider. The booking remains valid and pending work remains visible. Process the same message twice. Check actual deduplication behaviour. Submit two bookings for the same slot concurrently. Verify the conflict rule. Record the mechanism, rationale, alternatives, accepted limitations and verification in an ADR. The architect approves the decision; AI helps prepare and challenge it. Your turn In two sentences, explain why “we have a queue” does not establish reliability and which test exposes the database-to-queue gap. Then change the assumption: email must confirm a booking. Which process states now need clarification? Try the HLD generator → · Record an ADR → · Explore resilience patterns → Sources and further verification AWS: transactional outbox and dual writes Mermaid flowchart syntax C4 diagram levels The review method and prompts are an ArchitectMentor editorial proposal. Prepared with AI assistance.

/en/foundations/adr/.title: ADR: a record of consequential decisions
/en/foundations/adr/.text: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a concise account of a decision with significant consequences. A basic record includes a title, status, context, decision and consequences. In practice, also record the options considered and the assumptions on which the decision depends. Fictional example: “We will use a queue instead of a synchronous call for reservation-change notifications. This tolerates brief provider outages, while introducing delivery latency and the need to handle retries.” When a decision changes, add a new ADR and record its relationship to the earlier one. That preserves the reason the solution took its current shape. Source: ADR Templates — common ADR elements ↗

/en/foundations/architecture-description.title: What does an architect describe?
/en/foundations/architecture-description.text: Architecture is the organisation of a solution and the relationships that matter to its goals and qualities. An architecture description supports discussion: it presents a system from the perspectives of people who make decisions, build it and carry the risk. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 specifies requirements for an architecture description and distinguishes that description from the architecture itself. It does not prescribe one notation or one design method. In practice: before drawing a diagram, write down the goal, stakeholders, important scenarios, constraints and quality concerns that could change the solution. Source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — scope ↗

/en/foundations/architecture-patterns/.title: Apply patterns to specific risks
/en/foundations/architecture-patterns/.text: Retry + circuit breaker When a dependency fails temporarily, use bounded retries with spacing and stop further calls during a sustained failure. Watch for retry storms across service layers. Transactional outbox When a state change and event publication must stay consistent, store the event in the database in the same transaction and publish it with a separate process. Consumers still need to handle duplicates. Rule: name the failure scenario and quality requirement before choosing a pattern. Each pattern brings operational cost and new states to handle. Sources: Microsoft — transient faults ↗ · Chris Richardson — transactional outbox ↗

/en/foundations/asynchronous-notificatio.title: Asynchronous communication: separate the order from its notification
/en/foundations/asynchronous-notificatio.text: Practice-inspired educational scenario. An order has been saved, but its informational email was not sent. This is not one failed operation. It is one completed business outcome and one incomplete auxiliary effect. Name the outcome first If order acceptance ends when the order record commits, that is the boundary of the business outcome. Email, SMS, a search index update or an analytics record can be effects of that outcome. Failure of an add-on must not turn a truthful “order accepted” into a misleading “please try again”. That is how duplicates are born. Asynchronous does not mean “put something on a queue and hope”. Saving the order and publishing a message are two writes. If the process dies between them, the order exists and the message does not. A durable intent to perform the work The simplest design can insert a pending-notification record in the same local transaction as the order. A worker reads it, sends the notification and records the result. When more consumers need events, the transactional outbox applies the same rule: the domain change and an outbox record commit atomically, while a separate relay publishes the record. The outbox closes the gap between the database and broker, but it does not make the system magically exactly-once. A relay can publish the same record again. The consumer needs a stable operation identifier and idempotency or deduplication. For email, decide whether a duplicate message is tolerable or must be suppressed. Retry is a decision, not a reflex retry only the failed task, not the whole business operation; use bounded attempts, backoff and jitter so a dependency outage is not amplified; after attempts are exhausted, retain the task for intervention and reconciliation rather than deleting the evidence; measure the age of the oldest pending task, attempt counts and permanent failures; tell the user the truth: the order was accepted and confirmation may arrive later. How to verify the decision Exercise three failures: mail is unavailable, the process terminates after the database commit, and the relay publishes twice. The outcome should be boring: one order, a durable task, controlled retries and at most one user-visible notification. Boring resilience is a compliment. Boundary: if notification is a legal or business condition of accepting the operation, it is not an auxiliary effect. Establish that contract before choosing the pattern. Further reading: AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Transactional outbox pattern . The guidance describes atomic event recording and the need for an idempotent consumer.

/en/foundations/bulkhead/.title: Bulkhead: isolate resources that can be exhausted
/en/foundations/bulkhead/.text: The bulkhead pattern partitions scarce resources between functions or customer groups. When one dependency slows down, its requests occupy their own connection pool, worker pool or queue. Other pools can continue to serve traffic. Business requirements and failure scenarios determine the boundary, not the name of a microservice. Fictional example: orders and reports call different services but share a pool of 40 connections. A slow reporting service occupies the pool and blocks orders. Separate concurrency limits and a bounded reporting queue keep the critical path available, at the cost of delayed reports. How do you decide? Identify the functions that must continue when another dependency fails. Measure load, response times, pool saturation and queue length for each function. Choose separate limits, timeouts and overload behaviour. Test a slowdown under representative traffic. Trade-off: separate pools can leave capacity unused and add operational parameters. Choose isolation boundaries according to the cost of failure. Source: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center — Bulkhead pattern ↗

/en/foundations/business-process-availab.title: Business-process availability: from green components to a user outcome
/en/foundations/business-process-availab.text: Learning goal: define service availability through the outcome promised to the user, rather than the number of green components. Fictional educational scenario. A portal accepts a request and returns an identifier. The API, database and broker respond, but a stopped consumer never takes the process to a terminal state. This is not an account of a particular organisation or incident. Two truthful answers can contradict each other The command-acceptance service may be available while the business process is not. These are two different commitments: acceptance — the system durably accepted the work and can identify it; completion — the work reached an agreed terminal state within the agreed time. If a dashboard combines those answers, green is not necessarily a lie. It is an answer to a question that is too small. An evidence ladder Layer Question Example evidence What it does not prove Process Is the component alive? Liveness, restart and resource use Readiness to serve traffic Dependency Can the component perform its step? Readiness, connectivity and permissions Completion of the whole process Progress Is accepted work moving? Oldest-work age, completion rate and permanent failures Correctness of the user outcome Outcome Does the user receive the promised service? Terminal-state SLI and a controlled synthetic journey The root cause of a failure All layers are useful. Outcome signals expose the failure; component signals help locate it. One chart need not pretend to be the whole architecture. Start with the process contract Name the accepted state and terminal states: success, rejection, cancellation or human intervention. Agree the measurement start, window and population. Do not invent a duration merely to give a dashboard a threshold. Carry a correlation identifier through queues, consumers and state stores. Keep confidential content out of metric labels. Measure latency and lack of progress. Queue depth alone can also rise during healthy traffic bursts. Define what happens after the threshold: limit intake, disclose delay, route to manual handling or stop the process. A safe end-to-end probe A synthetic journey needs a separate identity, harmless data, bounded frequency and controlled cleanup. It must verify the terminal state, not merely an HTTP response. For operations that create obligations, use an isolated test path instead of generating “monitoring orders” in production. Monitoring can become a customer too; it merely tends not to pay the invoices. The negative test Stop a consumer in a controlled environment and expect: component checks to state precisely what still works; progress measures to detect ageing work; the outcome SLO to consume budget according to the contract; recovery not to create duplicate effects; operators to account for every accepted item. Boundary of the technique An end-to-end probe does not replace diagnostics, security tests or queue-capacity decisions. An SLO does not repair a process; it tells you when the observed outcome departs from the accepted promise. That promise has to exist first. Practise the decision on a stalled process → Sources and method basis: Google SRE — Monitoring Distributed Systems ; Google SRE Workbook — Implementing SLOs ; OpenTelemetry — traces . The evidence ladder and scenario are original ArchitectMentor work. Sources checked 19 October 2026.

/en/foundations/c4/.title: C4: show the system at the right level
/en/foundations/c4/.text: The C4 model helps move from a system’s environment towards implementation detail. Its levels are system context, containers, components and code. In C4, a “container” is a deployable application or data store; it does not have to be a Docker container. Context Who uses the system, and which other systems does it interact with? Containers Which applications and data stores make up the system, and how does information flow between them? Components How are responsibilities divided inside one application? Code How is a selected part implemented when that level of detail helps? You do not need all four levels. Start with context and containers, then add detail wherever it answers a specific question. Source: C4 model — diagram types ↗

/en/foundations/change-impact-analysis/.title: Change impact analysis: hardware, apps and system boundaries
/en/foundations/change-impact-analysis/.text: Replacing a device can preserve the architecture while still requiring an impact assessment. Change impact analysis establishes what stays the same, what changes and what evidence supports that conclusion. Start with three questions App: do the code, libraries and peripherals work in the new environment? Identity and security: do sign-in, permissions and device management preserve expected rules? Communication: do API contracts, connections and the complete user journey still work? Example Practice-inspired educational scenario: a company replaces tablets while user tasks and the server stay the same. A small trial checks sign-in, work-order processing and result submission. Actual differences define the next steps. Assume neither zero impact nor a complete redesign. How can C4 help? A context diagram shows the system, users and external systems. A container diagram can show the device app, server and communication. Comparing before and after can reveal a new dependency or trust boundary. C4 describes architecture; it does not certify compatibility. Record the decision Capture scope, unchanged and changed elements, representative trial results, open questions and a way back. If boundaries, contracts or important quality properties change, extend the review accordingly. If they do not, support that conclusion with evidence. Limits One successful test does not prove every device model and configuration compatible. Choose a sample reflecting actual use. An architecture model does not replace running the app on the target device. Practise: new tablets → · Source: C4 context diagrams

/en/foundations/conditional-architecture.title: Conditional architecture approval is not a release sign-off
/en/foundations/conditional-architecture.text: Learning goal: distinguish conditional acceptance of an architectural direction from permission to launch a service, and turn each condition into an accountable, verifiable obligation: owner, evidence, verifier and decision gate. Fictional educational scenario. A review group accepts a design on two conditions: demonstrate that access can be revoked effectively, and recover the complete user journey after a failure. The minutes end with “IT will confirm compliance”. Delivery reads this as a green light. Nobody has agreed who runs the checks, who assesses the evidence or what happens if a test fails. This is a model example, not an account of an incident at a particular organisation. Three options, three different consequences Option Benefit Risk A. Accept without qualification and move the conditions to a task list. Work starts quickly. No explicit gate stops launch when evidence is missing; a declaration may be mistaken for completion. B. Stop all work until both checks are complete. Uncertainty is not mistaken for proof. Work independent of the checks is blocked, increasing waiting costs. C. Conditionally accept a defined scope but keep the launch gate closed until evidence is verified. Reversible work can proceed while the risk is controlled. Conditions need active tracking and an explicitly authorised gate decision-maker. Choose C in this scenario , provided the missing evidence does not undermine the feasibility of the architecture itself. Accepting a direction, authorising implementation and authorising launch may be three separate decisions. A single “approved” status should not collapse them. Give every condition an execution contract Record six fields for each condition: what must be true , who owns fulfilment , which artefact proves it , who verifies and accepts that evidence , before which gate , and what happens on failure . A due date and decision ID help with traceability but cannot replace acceptance criteria. Condition and criterion Delivery owner Evidence and verifier Gate Access revocation: after privileges are withdrawn, a protected operation is denied even from a previously active session. Owner of the identity mechanism. Positive and negative test record; reviewed by the security-control verifier. Before users are admitted. Service recovery: after a controlled failure, the agreed user journey works, not merely the database process. Owner of service continuity. Recovery exercise report with outcomes, limitations and deviations; reviewed by the operational-readiness verifier. Before production launch. These are illustrative roles , not a universal governance policy. The review coordinator maintains decision coherence and escalations; that does not automatically make them the control owner, test executor or risk acceptor. The final gate belongs to the role authorised by the organisation's actual governance. Write a decision someone can execute Example decision note: “We accept the architectural direction for reversible work. This does not authorise service launch. Before the launch gate, the two control owners must provide agreed test results; designated verifiers must confirm the acceptance criteria. Missing evidence or a failed test leaves the condition open and returns the matter to the authorised decision-maker: change the design, repeat the test or explicitly change the scope. Silence is not acceptance.” The minimum flow is proposal → conditional acceptance → evidence and verification → gate decision . Keep the decision version, date, outstanding conditions and evidence links in the record. Do not mark a condition closed merely because its deadline passed or its delivery task was marked done. When is C the wrong choice? If an essential mechanism may not be feasible at all, the condition could invalidate the design. Do not approve a direction whose viability depends on that unknown: commission an experiment or proof of feasibility and revisit the options. Conversely, a minor improvement should not automatically block launch; record it as follow-up work with an owner and due date. The consequence of a failed condition, not emphatic wording in meeting minutes, should determine the gate. Your two-minute decision An owner submits a screenshot saying “test complete”, but it does not describe the negative test case. Launch is tomorrow. Can the coordinator close the condition? Not on the screenshot alone. Compare the evidence with the criterion, obtain the designated verifier's assessment, and keep the gate closed or refer an exception to the authorised risk decision-maker. Coordination is not a substitute for that decision. Continue learning: ADR — decisions and consequences ; Quality-attribute scenarios — testable criteria ; Practice — responsibility boundaries ; Anti-pattern — temporary integration without an exit decision . The latter two cover different cases but reinforce the distinction between responsibility and a verifiable condition. Primary sources (checked 13 October 2026): Official ADR process guidance — context, decision, consequences, status and ownership; ADR process FAQ — responsibility for maintaining decisions; Public security and privacy control assessment methodology — planning and assessing control evidence. The six-field condition contract, A–C options and examples are original educational synthesis; these sources do not prescribe one mandatory architecture approval process for every organisation.

/en/foundations/do-we-need-data-replicat.title: Do we actually need a data replica?
/en/foundations/do-we-need-data-replicat.text: Learning goal: decide when a data replica delivers a necessary architectural property and when it merely adds cost and risk. Fictional educational scenario. A proposed service includes another copy of a database “for performance and safety”. No workload evidence, acceptable data age, failover process or owner for discrepancies has been defined. This is a model exercise, not an account of a particular project. Which property are we trying to achieve? A replica may offload reads, reduce distance to data or support an alternate service path. A copy is not automatically high availability: without tested application failover it may not shorten an outage. It is not a backup either: erroneous updates and deletions can propagate. Option Appropriate when What to verify A. No replica; optimise the source Poor queries, indexing or needless reads cause the bottleneck. Do measured latency and throughput meet objectives without another copy? B. Read-only replica Reporting reads compete with transactional workloads. What replication lag is acceptable? How will read-after-write and failures work? C. Failover replica Recovery objectives justify another node or site. How will failure detection, split-brain prevention, promotion and failback be tested? Neither B nor C is the default. Without measurable demand and recovery objectives, define acceptance criteria before adding a database. Better indexes, a carefully governed cache or an asynchronous reporting pipeline might be suitable alternatives, each with distinct consistency and operations trade-offs. Evidence gate Before approval, record baseline workload , freshness requirements , consistency expectations , RPO/RTO , failover design , data scope and retention , and operational cost . Measure replication lag under load and rehearse failover and return. Queries requiring authoritative current state should use the source of truth. Example ADR: “Do not introduce a replica at launch. First baseline workload and latency; define allowed staleness and recovery objectives. Consider a read replica only if source optimisation demonstrably misses the SLO. A high-availability replica needs a separate tested failover and failback decision.” Related reading: RPO/RTO recovery drill , conditional approval , SLO and error budgets .

/en/foundations/evolving-api-contracts/.title: Evolving an API contract: compatibility needs evidence
/en/foundations/evolving-api-contracts/.text: Adding a response field looks harmless: nothing has been removed, so the change should be backward compatible. It should. In integration work, “should” is often the most expensive word in the plan. Learning goal: distinguish compatibility of a description or wire format from compatibility of running consumers, then plan an API change using evidence. Three layers of compatibility Layer Question Example risk Source Does client code still compile? An SDK generator changes a signature or type. Wire Can an old client receive and deserialize the new response? Strict mode rejects an unknown property. Semantic Does the client still receive the behaviour a reasonable developer expected? A new enum value or changed default selects the wrong branch. Google AIP-180 makes this distinction between source, wire and semantic compatibility. It also warns that compatibility guidance is indicative rather than proof for every technology stack. Optional does not mean irrelevant An optional request field means an old client need not send it. An optional response field means the server may omit it. Neither statement proves that a particular client accepts an unknown property or handles a new value safely. An additive change is usually safer than removing a field, but it can expose a hidden contract: strict deserialization, an exhaustive enum switch, a database length limit or logic coupled to an undocumented format. An API contract includes behaviour, not just an OpenAPI file. A pre-release matrix Change Initial assessment What to verify New optional response field Usually additive Unknown fields, generated models, proxies and validators. New response enum value Elevated risk Fallback branches and generated-code behaviour. Changed default value Semantically incompatible Clients that omit the field. Optional field becomes required Incompatible Every existing request producer. Existing value changes format Semantically risky Parsers, validation, indexes and column lengths. How to verify an API change Define compatibility rules. Record evolution rules: whether clients ignore unknown fields, whether enums are extensible and how long a version is supported. Inventory consumers. Owner, library version, deserialization mode and upgrade window matter more than the endpoint count. Test representative versions. Replay a response containing the new field in contract tests and run the oldest supported client. Limit exposure. Roll out gradually, observe deserialization failures and retain a way to stop exposing the field. Version when existing compatibility rules cannot be maintained. Introduce a new version when existing behaviour cannot be preserved or consumer upgrades cannot be controlled. Fictional educational example: a server adds deliveryWindow to an order response. OpenAPI does not mark it as required, but an older mobile app rejects every unknown property. Before broad rollout, the team tests a supported client version, changes its deserialization rule and only then exposes the field progressively. Boundary of this advice Not every integration needs public versioning. When the producer controls every consumer and can enforce a coordinated update, a simpler process may be enough. The team must still verify the actual version mix during deployment. “It is only a field” is not a migration strategy. Practise the new-field decision → Primary sources (checked 3 October 2026): Google AIP-180 — Backwards compatibility ; Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines — contracts and versioning . The matrices, example and verification procedure are original educational material.

/en/foundations/frameworks-and-models/.title: Standards, methods, languages and models serve different purposes
/en/foundations/frameworks-and-models/.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 Requirements for architecture descriptions: helps establish the viewpoints and information needed for a useful description. TOGAF A standard and approach for enterprise architecture, including the ADM method. It supports work from a business need through change planning and governance. ArchiMate A language for modelling enterprise architecture. It helps show relationships between business, application and technology layers. C4 + ADR Views of a solution and records of decisions. They complement broader approaches when you need to explain a particular system and its trade-offs. Choose the elements that help a stakeholder make a decision. A diagram without a question to answer quickly becomes decoration. Sources: The Open Group — TOGAF ↗ · The Open Group — ArchiMate ↗

/en/foundations/graceful-degradation/.title: Graceful degradation: preserve the core function
/en/foundations/graceful-degradation/.text: Graceful degradation deliberately limits features during a failure while preserving a safe, useful part of the service. It begins by separating essential functions from optional ones, rather than ignoring errors. Example Practice-inspired educational scenario: a document was generated, but saving an optional copy failed. The user can still read and download the document. Separate the two outcomes: “Your document is ready. The copy was not saved.” Design the boundary Define success for the core operation and identify features that may be limited. Bound dependency waits so an optional feature does not block the entire response. Preserve the available result and clearly disclose the limitation. Monitor failure and recovery without recording confidential content. What does this not solve? It does not guarantee that a copy will be saved later. That needs a separate durable mechanism and error handling. It also does not replace resource isolation: if an optional feature exhausts a shared connection pool, catching an exception may not protect the service. Mandatory functions are different An order requiring durable storage is not successfully accepted just because a screen displays confirmation. Access control cannot simply be skipped during a failure either. Requirements establish what can degrade and what must end in confirmed success or explicit failure. Practise a storage failure → · Source: Azure — self-preservation and graceful degradation

/en/foundations/hld-review-checklist/.title: Five questions before an HLD review
/en/foundations/hld-review-checklist/.text: What business problem are we solving, and how will we know we succeeded? Which facts have been confirmed, and which are still assumptions? Which quality concerns — availability, performance, security, data and cost — change the design? Which decisions are reversible, and which require an ADR and explicit acceptance of risk? How will we test the most important assumption before implementation becomes expensive? You can use this checklist to review an HLD. The ADR guide explains how to record a consequential decision.

/en/foundations/idempotency-lookup-compe.title: Idempotency, lookup and compensation: three different jobs
/en/foundations/idempotency-lookup-compe.text: A missing response may mean the request never arrived, is still running or completed with a lost response. A timeout does not establish the outcome. Three mechanisms answer three different questions. Idempotency: can I repeat safely? Repeating the same operation should not create an additional effect within the API’s guaranteed scope. A stable identifier distinguishes a retry from a new business attempt. Define scope, retention, concurrent requests and identifier reuse with different payloads. An identifier without provider-side handling does not guarantee safety. Lookup: what happened to the original operation? Checking by operation identifier can establish success, confirmed failure or an unknown result. “Not found” need not mean “not executed”: its meaning depends on completeness, delay and the contract. Unresolved operations require reconciliation rather than a blind new request. Compensation: how do I correct a business effect? Compensation is a new operation correcting an earlier effect. It can fail and needs its own identity, preconditions and retry handling. Reversal in one API does not necessarily mean refund or cancellation in another. Example and limits Practice-inspired educational scenario: payment was collected but it is unknown whether a booking exists. This example’s contract permits bounded idempotent retries, then lookup, and payment reversal only after unequivocal confirmation that no booking was created. This is an exercise assumption, not a universal payment procedure. Do not create another booking after confirmed success; retain unknown outcomes for reconciliation. Practise an unknown outcome → · Source: AWS — safe retries

/en/foundations/quality-attribute-scenar.title: Quality-attribute scenarios: from adjective to measure
/en/foundations/quality-attribute-scenar.text: “The system must be fast, secure and easy to change” sounds useful but does not yet guide a design or a test. A quality-attribute scenario turns an adjective into observable behaviour by naming the source, stimulus, environment, affected artefact, expected response and a measurable response threshold. Six parts of a useful scenario Source: who or what causes the situation — a user, operator, external system or failure. Stimulus: the specific event, such as a traffic increase, dependency failure or rule change. Environment: the conditions — normal operation, peak load, deployment or disaster recovery. Artefact: the part of the system affected. Response: what the system does after the stimulus. Response measure: the threshold that makes success testable. Fictional modifiability example: when a team changes the name and allowed values of a field used by two application versions during a normal release, the system supports a compatible transition and code rollback without losing writes; no outage is required and data discrepancies remain at zero for an agreed observation window. Why is a quality label insufficient? Two people can interpret “high availability” differently. One may mean an individual API is reachable; another may mean the customer completes an end-to-end journey. A scenario exposes that difference before a technology is chosen. It also reveals trade-offs: faster change may require temporary support for two contracts, while lower cost may limit redundancy. ISO/IEC 25010:2023 provides a product quality model, but a catalogue of characteristics does not replace system-specific requirements. Software Engineering Institute material uses scenarios in Quality Attribute Workshops so stakeholders can generate and prioritise situations involving a stimulus, environment and response. How does a scenario support a decision? Start with an event that matters to a stakeholder, not with a product or pattern. State the environment and measure. “95% below 300 ms at 500 requests per second” is a different problem from the same latency without a load condition. Compare options by response and cost. Record in the ADR which scenarios the decision supports and which trade-offs remain. Turn the measure into a test, production observation or failure exercise. If the result cannot be checked, the scenario remains too vague. Illustrative ADR excerpt: Context: a rolling release leaves two application versions running together. Quality scenario: after a schema change, both versions serve traffic correctly and code rollback loses no data. Decision: use expand–migrate–contract stages. Verification: mixed-version test, missing-value checks and a rollback rehearsal before the old field is removed. Project question: which three situations — peak load, dependency failure, contract change, security incident or recovery — truly shape your architecture, and what measure will decide success? Sources: Software Engineering Institute — Quality Attribute Workshop Collection ; ISO/IEC 25010:2023 — Product quality model . The system details, values and ADR are original fictional examples.

/en/foundations/retry-budget-single-owne.title: Can retries make an overloaded dependency worse?
/en/foundations/retry-budget-single-owne.text: Learning goal: assign retry ownership and a shared attempt budget rather than multiplying requests to an overloaded dependency. Scenario: nine calls instead of one This is a fictional educational example, not a report of a production incident. An API calls an intermediary service, which reads a catalogue. Both calling layers allow up to three attempts, including the first request. If the catalogue keeps failing, one user operation can generate nine catalogue calls (3 × 3). Extra traffic hits the dependency precisely when it has the least spare capacity. Three design options A — retry at every layer. Simple locally, but attempts multiply across layers and tail latency can increase. B — one retry owner. The catalogue adapter retries safe reads; upstream callers propagate one deadline and never restart the entire chain. C — no retry. Appropriate when repeating an operation can cause an irreversible side effect or the previous outcome cannot be determined. Conditional decision Choose B for reads , provided we verify the behavior of the SDK, HTTP client, gateway and intermediaries. The attempt budget applies to the user operation, not independently to each layer. Capped exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retry storms; concurrency limits protect the catalogue from queued demand. Once the shared deadline expires, no further attempt is allowed. Writes require an idempotency key or a reliable outcome-lookup contract; otherwise automatic retries remain disabled. How do we prove it works? Trace the real API → intermediary → catalogue path and inventory retry behavior in every SDK and gateway. Inject HTTP 429 and 503 responses, both with and without Retry-After. This header suggests a delay; it does not authorize retries beyond the operation deadline. Measure catalogue calls per user operation, p95/p99 latency, concurrent requests and recovery time after failures stop. Verify that attempts stop at the budget and unsafe writes are not repeated without a safe contract. Architect's question: if the gateway and SDK both retry independently, which layer owns the decision and who accounts for the total attempt cost? Primary references Amazon Builders’ Library — Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter RFC 9110, §10.2.3 — Retry-After RFC 6585, §4 — 429 Too Many Requests Related topics: idempotency and outcome lookup, bulkhead, and SLO error budgets.

/en/foundations/rpo-rto-recovery-drill/.title: RPO, RTO and a full-service recovery drill
/en/foundations/rpo-rto-recovery-drill/.text: RPO and RTO often appear in a table next to the word “backup”. That is not yet a recovery plan. Start by stating what must return: a database, an API or the user's ability to finish a task. Two different measures RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss expressed as time: how old the last valid recovered state may be. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum elapsed time to restore the agreed function after service interruption. Define when the clock starts, which function counts and who accepts the result. RPO is not a backup schedule; RTO is not a machine boot time. Fictional example. A portal targets an RPO of five minutes and an RTO of 30 minutes. An outage is detected at 10:00. Its last valid restored write is from 09:52, and users can again submit and retrieve an application at 10:42. The achieved values are at least eight minutes of lost writes and 42 minutes of downtime. Both targets are missed even if a database backup job ran at 09:55. Why multiple stores change the calculation Metadata in a database, attachments in object storage and messages in a queue do not automatically form one recoverable transaction. You may retrieve a row without its file or replay a message already processed. Define a business identifier for reconciliation, a way to detect missing items and a policy for duplicates. If a technically consistent point is unavailable, describe compensation and how losses are approved. A useful recovery drill Select the critical user journey and all of its dependencies. Distinguish full service from a limited mode. In an isolated environment simulate loss of the primary region. Check that backups, keys and instructions remain accessible without it. Restore a representative volume of data and services; time the interval from detection to a successful user journey, rather than until “the server responds”. Reconcile records, files and messages. Count the latest available write, missing objects, duplicates and work requiring manual completion. Compare the results with the objectives. Assign an owner and deadline to every gap; repeat after material architecture changes. Choosing more frequent replication, backups, active redundancy or a manual workaround depends on the cost of lost data and downtime. Each option carries different cost and risk; none removes the need to rehearse. Replication can faithfully copy a bad write too. Question for your project: when did you last restore the complete user journey, and what RPO and RTO did you measure rather than declare?

/en/foundations/saas-architecture-due-di.title: SaaS architecture due diligence: what the customer needs to know
/en/foundations/saas-architecture-due-di.text: Buying SaaS reduces the technology the customer designs and operates. It still leaves a system spanning organisations: the user channel, identity, data, integration and business continuity. 1. Review behaviour and ownership The useful question is which boundaries and risks the customer owns or depends on. A provider's implementation language and internal component names may be irrelevant when the customer neither operates them nor relies on a particular implementation. The service contract and its evidence matter whenever a change can affect the customer. 2. Connect a requirement to evidence For each material requirement, name the responsible party, service scope, observable result and acceptance evidence. The customer and provider may share a task; explicitly divide it rather than writing “IT is responsible”. A declaration is an input to review, not a completed test. 3. Seven areas of SaaS review Area Establish Example evidence Responsibility Who operates each component and responds to failure Responsibility matrix with named owners Data Processing location, retention, isolation, backup and export Data flow, policy and export test IAM Federation, roles, privileged and support access Sign-in and access-revocation test Integration APIs, versioning, limits and errors Contract and failure/negative test Quality requirements Availability, latency, capacity, RTO/RPO SLA/SLO scope, measurement and recovery drill Operations Telemetry, status, incidents and changes Runbook, correlation and escalation path Exit Data portability and service termination Export format and exit rehearsal 4. Availability and recovery need a boundary An SLA has limited value when the measured function and perspective are unspecified. RTO and RPO need a defined scope of data and functions. A customer-owned channel can give the complete user journey a different recovery time from the provider service alone. Specify maintenance and exclusions as well as the target. 5. Observability belongs in the operating contract The customer need not see every internal log. It needs enough information to understand service and integration health: status, relevant metrics, error codes, correlation identifiers, incident communication and escalation. A successful HTTP request alone does not demonstrate a completed business process. 6. Customer-hosted components change the review An agent, terminal, connector, gateway or data plane in the customer environment adds architecture the customer must operate. Establish version compatibility, supported OS/runtime, upgrade ownership, network requirements, telemetry and rollback. Assess the actual deployment model rather than treating it as a remote website. 7. Exit is an architectural requirement Managed services can remain a sound choice while some dependencies are hard to move. Establish export format, completeness, delivery time, deletion handling and integration/identity shutdown. Test an export before the process becomes dependent on the provider. From a question to evidence Fictional example: a business-agreed four-hour RTO covers the customer channel, IAM, SaaS and integration. A vendor database-recovery declaration alone does not prove that objective. Agree owners, drill conditions and measurement start/end points. Four hours is not a universal target. For data, test export and readability outside the service. For access, check role revocation, existing sessions and privileged support access. For integration, examine missing responses, limits and contract versions. Record the result, service version and unknowns. Scale evidence to process criticality and assign acceptance of remaining risk. Decision rule: Do we know every boundary, risk and behaviour we own or depend on, and do we have evidence for it? Sources and method Primary sources checked 11 October 2026: Azure SaaS design principles and design methodology . They explain responsibility and service-design principles; they do not prove any particular vendor's capabilities. The seven-area checklist and responsibility → requirement → evidence matrix are ArchitectMentor editorial synthesis. Prepared with AI assistance.
